claim: Double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) is effective for silencing a wide variety of genes.
source: Since double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) is effective for silencing a wide variety of genes, all genes are typically considered equivalent targets for such RNA interference (RNAi).
evidence: This is a general statement about dsRNA effectiveness that is part of established scientific knowledge in the field of RNAi.

claim: Loss of some regulators of RNAi in C. elegans can selectively impair the silencing of some genes.
source: Yet, loss of some regulators of RNAi in the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans can selectively impair the silencing of some genes.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing differential requirements for RNAi regulators.

claim: RDE-10, MUT-16, and NRDE-3 work together such that any two are required for silencing one somatic gene (unc-22), but each is singly required for silencing another somatic gene (bli-1).
source: In this network, the Maelstrom domain-containing protein RDE-10, the intrinsically disordered protein MUT-16, and the Argonaute protein NRDE-3 work together so that any two are required for silencing one somatic gene, but each is singly required for silencing another somatic gene, where only the requirement for NRDE-3 can be overcome by enhanced dsRNA processing.
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1 and 2, demonstrating differential genetic requirements for silencing bli-1 versus unc-22.

claim: The requirement for NRDE-3 can be overcome by enhanced dsRNA processing.
source: In this network, the Maelstrom domain-containing protein RDE-10, the intrinsically disordered protein MUT-16, and the Argonaute protein NRDE-3 work together so that any two are required for silencing one somatic gene, but each is singly required for silencing another somatic gene, where only the requirement for NRDE-3 can be overcome by enhanced dsRNA processing.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 3 showing that loss of ERI-1 or overexpression of RDE-4 can bypass the need for NRDE-3.

claim: Changing cis-regulatory elements of the target gene can reduce the dependence on NRDE-3.
source: Quantitative models and their exploratory simulations led us to find that (1) changing cis-regulatory elements of the target gene can reduce the dependence on NRDE-3
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 5 showing that swapping 3' cis-regulatory regions affects NRDE-3 requirements.

claim: Animals can recover from silencing in non-dividing cells.
source: Quantitative models and their exploratory simulations led us to find that (1) changing cis-regulatory elements of the target gene can reduce the dependence on NRDE-3, (2) animals can recover from silencing in non-dividing cells
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6A showing recovery from unc-22 silencing after a pulse of RNAi.

claim: Cleavage and tailing of mRNAs with UG dinucleotides are enriched within 'pUG zones' matching the dsRNA.
source: Quantitative models and their exploratory simulations led us to find that (1) changing cis-regulatory elements of the target gene can reduce the dependence on NRDE-3, (2) animals can recover from silencing in non-dividing cells, and (3) cleavage and tailing of mRNAs with UG dinucleotides, which makes them templates for amplifying small RNAs, are enriched within 'pUG zones' matching the dsRNA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 6C showing pUG RNA detection patterns.

claim: Double-stranded RNA can trigger RNA interference to degrade mRNA of matching sequence in many organisms.
source: Double-stranded RNA (dsRNA) can trigger the conserved mechanism of RNA interference (RNAi) to degrade mRNA of matching sequence (Fire et al., 1998), and thus silence gene expression, in many organisms.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fire et al., 1998 and represents established knowledge in the field.

claim: dsRNA-based drugs are useful in crops, insects, and humans.
source: This conservation has made dsRNA-based drugs useful in crops (Das and Sherif, 2020), insects (Vogel et al., 2018), and humans (Zhu et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published work.

claim: Long dsRNA is imported through the transmembrane protein SID-1.
source: Long dsRNA is imported through the transmembrane protein SID-1 (Feinberg and Hunter, 2003; Winston et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: dsRNA is bound by the dsRNA-binding protein RDE-4.
source: after which it is bound by the dsRNA-binding protein RDE-4 (Tabara et al., 2002)
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: RDE-4 recruits the endonuclease DCR-1 to cleave long dsRNA into smaller dsRNAs.
source: which recruits the endonuclease DCR-1 (Knight and Bass, 2001) to cleave the long dsRNA into smaller dsRNAs (Parker et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: The primary Argonaute protein RDE-1 cleaves one strand of the smaller dsRNA.
source: The primary Argonaute protein RDE-1 (Parrish and Fire, 2001; Tabara et al., 1999) cleaves one strand of the smaller dsRNA (Steiner et al., 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Target mRNAs are cleaved and the 5′ fragments are stabilized through the addition of 3′ UG-dinucleotide repeats by the nucleotidyltransferase RDE-3 to form pUG RNAs.
source: After recognition by RDE-1-bound siRNAs, the target mRNAs are cleaved and the 5′ fragments are stabilized through the addition of 3′ UG-dinucleotide repeats (Preston et al., 2019) by the nucleotidyltransferase RDE-3 (Chen et al., 2005) to form pUG RNAs (Shukla et al., 2020)
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: pUG RNAs act as templates for the amplification of 2° siRNAs.
source: which act as templates for the amplification of 2° siRNAs (Pak and Fire, 2007) by RNA-dependent RNA polymerases.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Amplification of silencing signals through the production of 2° siRNAs is facilitated by MUT-16, RDE-10, and their interactors.
source: This amplification of silencing signals through the production of 2° siRNAs is facilitated by the intrinsically disordered protein MUT-16 (Phillips et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2011), the Maelstrom domain-containing protein RDE-10 (Yang et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2012), and their interactors (Phillips et al., 2012; Uebel et al., 2018; Yang et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to published work.

claim: 2° siRNAs are bound by one of several Argonautes.
source: These 2° siRNAs are bound by one of several Argonautes (Yigit et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Co-transcriptional silencing of the target gene in the nucleus requires a nuclear Argonaute (e.g., NRDE-3).
source: and/or co-transcriptional silencing of the target gene in the nucleus, which requires a nuclear Argonaute (e.g., NRDE-3 Guang et al., 2008 in somatic cells).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Past studies have highlighted gene-specific differences in the efficacy of RNAi under different conditions.
source: Although it is difficult to compare the silencing of two different genes by controlling all relevant variables, past studies have highlighted gene-specific differences in the efficacy of RNAi under different conditions (e.g., when RNAi is enhanced through the loss of the exonuclease ERI-1; Kennedy et al., 2004, when nuclear silencing is blocked in somatic cells through loss of NRDE-3; Raman et al., 2017, or when different concentrations of dsRNA are used; Zhuang and Hunter, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Five isolates with a mutation in mut-16 failed to silence bli-1 but retained unc-22 silencing.
source: Of five isolates with a mutation in mut-16, four (jam138, jam140, jam141, and jam247) failed to silence bli-1 (blue) but retained unc-22 silencing (orange).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The mut-16(jam139) rde-10(jam248) double mutant failed to silence both bli-1 and unc-22.
source: The other mutant failed to silence both genes and additionally had a mutation in rde-10 (mut-16(jam139) rde-10(jam248)).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: mut-16(jam148) single mutants show unc-22 silencing but not bli-1 silencing.
source: Mutants created using genome editing recapitulated the selective silencing of unc-22 in mut-16(−) single mutants (mut-16(jam148))
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: mut-16(jam148) rde-10(jam206) double mutants fail to silence both bli-1 and unc-22.
source: and the failure to silence both genes in mut-16(−) rde-10(−) double mutants (mut-16(jam148) rde-10(jam206)).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: rde-10(jam196) mutants show unc-22 silencing but not bli-1 silencing.
source: Using genome editing to recreate the jam248 mutation, which is expected to make a mutant protein (RDE-10(S228F)) that disrupts the Maelstrom domain (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1), resulted in animals (rde-10(jam196)) that showed unc-22 silencing but not bli-1 silencing.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The Ser228Phe mutation is expected to disrupt the Maelstrom domain of RDE-10.
source: This missense mutation (Ser228Phe) is expected to disrupt the Maelstrom domain of RDE-10 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is based on structural modeling shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: 1° siRNA production and RDE-1-mediated recognition of the mRNA is likely not sufficient to cause silencing of most genes.
source: Since unc-22 is a particularly sensitive target for RNAi (Fire et al., 1998), this lack of unc-22 silencing in the absence of two regulators with roles in the amplification of 2° siRNAs suggests that 1° siRNA production and RDE-1-mediated recognition of the mRNA is likely not sufficient to cause silencing of most genes.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data showing that mut-16(null) rde-10(null) double mutants fail to silence unc-22.

claim: MUT-16 and RDE-10 are redundantly or additively required for silencing unc-22.
source: These observations suggest that MUT-16 and RDE-10 are redundantly or additively required for silencing unc-22 and that the Maelstrom domain of RDE-10 is required for this function.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data showing differential requirements for these proteins.

claim: The Maelstrom domain of RDE-10 is required for its function in unc-22 silencing.
source: These observations suggest that MUT-16 and RDE-10 are redundantly or additively required for silencing unc-22 and that the Maelstrom domain of RDE-10 is required for this function.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data showing that the Ser228Phe mutation affects silencing.

claim: MUT-16 and RDE-10 act in parallel downstream of RDE-1 to promote the amplification of 2° siRNA.
source: Since the primary Argonaute RDE-1 is required for the silencing of all somatic targets (Figure 1A; Parrish and Fire, 2001; Tabara et al., 1999), including unc-22, we propose that MUT-16 and RDE-10 act in parallel downstream of RDE-1 to promote the amplification of 2° siRNA.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on experimental data and cited literature.

claim: Animals that lack MUT-16, RDE-10, or NRDE-3 fail to silence bli-1 but not unc-22.
source: Animals that lack MUT-16 (Figure 1D), RDE-10 (Figure 1D) or the somatic nuclear Argonaute NRDE-3 (Raman et al., 2017) fail to silence bli-1 but not unc-22.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 1D and citation to published work.

claim: rde-10(−); nrde-3(−) double mutants fail to silence unc-22.
source: However, rde-10(−); nrde-3(−) double mutants fail to silence unc-22 (Yang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: All single mutants (mut-16, rde-10, or nrde-3) failed to silence bli-1 but silenced unc-22.
source: As expected, all single mutants failed to silence bli-1 but silenced unc-22.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: All double mutants (mut-16/rde-10, mut-16/nrde-3, rde-10/nrde-3) failed to silence both bli-1 and unc-22.
source: Surprisingly, all double mutants failed to silence both bli-1 and unc-22 (Figures 1D and 2B).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1D and 2B.

claim: The requirement for any two of MUT-16, RDE-10, or NRDE-3 suggests that the RNAi pathway cannot be strictly parallel downstream of RDE-1.
source: This requirement for any two of MUT-16, RDE-10, or NRDE-3 suggests that the RNAi pathway cannot be strictly parallel downstream of RDE-1 (see Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data and modeling.

claim: 145 of 100,000 simulated parameter sets satisfied all experimental constraints for the intersecting network model.
source: Of the 100,000 sets of parameters simulated, 145 sets satisfied all experimental constraints (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Only thresholds for bli-1 silencing that are less than ~5.5× the threshold for unc-22 silencing were supported by the model.
source: Finally, only thresholds for bli-1 silencing that are less than ~5.5× the threshold for unc-22 silencing were supported despite the allowed range of up to 100× (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Reducing the availability of unc-22 dsRNA revealed a graded silencing response: mut-16(−)<rde-10(−)<nrde-3(−).
source: Consistent with different quantitative contributions to silencing by each regulator, reducing the availability of unc-22 dsRNA revealed a graded silencing response: mut-16(−)<rde-10(−)<nrde-3(−) (Figure 2E; ~5% silencing in mut-16(jam148), ~15% in rde-10(jam206), and ~70% in nrde-3(jam205)).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Partial silencing of unc-54 is observable in the absence of NRDE-3 but not MUT-16 or RDE-10.
source: Consistent with the possibility of differential contributions from each regulator for different targets (Figure 2D), while partial silencing is observable in the absence of NRDE-3 but not MUT-16 or RDE-10 when the muscle gene unc-54 is targeted (Figure 2F, left)
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Partial silencing of dpy-7 is observed in the absence of MUT-16 but not NRDE-3 or RDE-10.
source: partial silencing is observed in the absence of MUT-16 but not NRDE-3 or RDE-10 when the hypodermal gene dpy-7 is targeted (Figure 2F, right).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Loss of ERI-1 enabled bli-1 silencing in animals lacking NRDE-3, but not in animals lacking RDE-10 or MUT-16.
source: Loss of ERI-1 enabled bli-1 silencing in animals lacking NRDE-3, but not in animals lacking RDE-10 or MUT-16 (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Loss of eri-1 was not sufficient for the complete rescue of unc-22 silencing in animals lacking any two of MUT-16, RDE-10, or NRDE-3.
source: Furthermore, loss of eri-1 was not sufficient for the complete rescue of unc-22 silencing in animals lacking any two of these three regulators (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Hemizygous males expressing rde-4(+) from a single-copy transgene was sufficient for rescuing both bli-1 and unc-22 silencing.
source: We found that even hemizygous males expressing rde-4(+) from a single-copy transgene driving expression in the germline and the intestine under the control of the mex-5 promoter (Marré et al., 2016) was sufficient for rescuing both bli-1 and unc-22 silencing (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Similar expression of rde-1(+) was not sufficient for rescuing silencing in rde-1(−) animals.
source: Similar expression of rde-1(+), however, was not sufficient for rescuing silencing in rde-1(−) animals (Figure 3D), suggesting that small amounts of RDE-4 but not RDE-1 are sufficient for RNAi.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Hypodermal expression of rde-4(+) was sufficient to enable bli-1 silencing in an otherwise rde-4(−); nrde-3(−) background.
source: This hypodermal expression of rde-4(+) was sufficient to enable bli-1 silencing in an otherwise rde-4(−); nrde-3(−) background (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Loss of ERI-1 and/or overexpression of RDE-4 could not compensate for the loss of RDE-10 or MUT-16 for bli-1 silencing.
source: However, loss of ERI-1 and/or overexpression of RDE-4 could not compensate for the loss of RDE-10 or MUT-16 for bli-1 silencing (Figure 3F)
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: RNAi can result in different residual concentrations of RNAs for different genes.
source: Under this simple model, we found that (1) RNAi can result in different residual concentrations of RNAs for different genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C)
evidence: This is based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Silencing can alter the ratio of pre-mRNA to mRNA.
source: (2) for a given gene, silencing can alter the ratio of pre-mRNA to mRNA (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, E)
evidence: This is based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D, E.

claim: Effective targeting of mRNA by primary or secondary small RNAs is required for strong silencing.
source: and (3) effective targeting of mRNA by primary or secondary small RNAs is required for strong silencing (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: The time to knockdown (τkd) and the duration of knockdown (tkd) are uncorrelated.
source: Overall, τkd and tkd were uncorrelated (Figure 4D), with cases of rapid but transient knockdown, which would necessitate multiple dosing of dsRNA for sustained effects.
evidence: This is based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The maximal amount of 2° siRNAs that accumulate is not correlated with strong silencing as measured by the minimal amount of mRNA during knockdown.
source: However, the maximal amount of 2° siRNAs that accumulate is not correlated with strong silencing as measured by the minimal amount of mRNA during knockdown (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 4E.

claim: An increase in transcription generally resulted in poorer knockdown through changes in both τkd and tkd.
source: Additionally, an increase in transcription generally resulted in poorer knockdown through changes in both τkd and tkd (Figure 4F)
evidence: This is based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Genes with higher mRNA turnover showed less efficient knockdown when exposed to a fixed amount of dsRNA.
source: When a fixed amount of dsRNA was exposed to different genes with the same amount of mRNA at steady state, genes with higher mRNA turnover rates showed less efficient knockdown (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Animals with the unc-22 3′cis sequence in place of the bli-1 3′cis showed a much reduced dependence on NRDE-3.
source: Animals with the unc-22 3′cis sequence in place of the bli-1 3′cis (bli-1p::bli-1::unc-22 3′cis) showed a much reduced dependence on NRDE-3 (Figure 5B)
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Animals with the bli-1 3′cis sequence downstream of the coding sequence of unc-22 showed substantial twitching even without unc-22 RNAi.
source: Animals with the bli-1 3′cis sequence downstream of the coding sequence of unc-22 (unc-22p::unc-22::bli-1 3′cis) showed substantial twitching even without unc-22 RNAi (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Silencing of GFP expressed from the bli-1p::gfp::cye-1 3′cis transgene was detectable in animals lacking NRDE-3.
source: Animals with this gene showed expression of GFP in the hypodermis, which is most easily visible in the head region and is detectably silenced by ingested gfp-dsRNA in a wild-type background (Figure 5C). Similar silencing was detectable in animals lacking NRDE-3 (Figure 5D)
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: Silencing of bli-1p::gfp in animals lacking MUT-16 or RDE-10 was much weaker than in wild type.
source: but the silencing in animals lacking MUT-16 or RDE-10 was much weaker (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: Two different genes expressed under the same promoter within the same tissue can have different requirements for silencing in response to dsRNA.
source: Together, these results reveal that two different genes expressed under the same promoter within the same tissue can have different requirements for silencing in response to dsRNA (bli-1 vs gfp under the control of bli-1p).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data comparing bli-1 and bli-1p::gfp silencing requirements.

claim: Animals exposed to a 1-hr pulse of unc-22 dsRNA showed ~80% silencing after the first 24 hr, which reached ~100% by day 3.
source: With this limited exposure to dsRNA, we observed only ~80% silencing after the first 24 hr, which reached ~100% by day 3, suggesting that it takes a couple of days after exposure to small amounts of dsRNA to observe complete silencing.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Silencing after a pulse of unc-22 dsRNA was only observed in ~50% of the animals on day 5, which dropped to ~36% by the eighth day after RNAi.
source: Consistent with recovery, silencing was only observed in ~50% of the animals on day 5, which dropped to ~36% by the eighth day after RNAi.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Animals that were continually fed unc-22 RNAi showed ~100% silencing even at day 7.
source: In contrast, animals that were continually fed unc-22 RNAi showed ~100% silencing even at day 7 (Figure 6A), suggesting that the RNAi machinery remains functional in aging animals.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: Body-wall muscle cells do not divide during adulthood.
source: Since the body-wall muscle cells – where unc-22 functions – do not divide during adulthood (Krause and Liu, 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Recovery from silencing cannot be explained by the dilution of dsRNA and/or RNA intermediates through cell division.
source: Since the body-wall muscle cells – where unc-22 functions – do not divide during adulthood (Krause and Liu, 2012), this observation of recovery from silencing cannot be explained by the dilution of dsRNA and/or RNA intermediates through cell division.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data and cited knowledge about muscle cell division.

claim: pUG RNAs were detected after cleavage within the unc-22 mRNA sequence that matches the dsRNA.
source: Consistent with the production of pUG RNAs upon targeting by 1° siRNAs, we detected pUG RNAs generated after cleavage within the unc-22 mRNA sequence that matches the dsRNA (Figure 6B, 0 kb 5′ primer).
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: All pUG RNAs detected using a 5′ primer ~1 kb upstream of the target sequence were larger than 1 kb.
source: Surprisingly, all pUG RNAs detected using a 5′ primer ~1 kb upstream of the target sequence were larger than 1 kb (Figure 6C, 1 kb 5′ primer), suggesting that there is a dearth of pUG RNA formation through cleavage within 1 kb upstream of sequences targeted by dsRNA.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: During RNAi in somatic cells, the addition of pUG tails is enriched within a zone on target mRNAs that share homology with the dsRNA trigger.
source: This lack of detectable pUG RNAs upstream suggests that, during RNAi in somatic cells, the addition of pUG tails is enriched within a zone on target mRNAs that share homology with the dsRNA trigger (pUG zone).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data showing the distribution of pUG RNAs.

claim: The requirement for NRDE-3 for silencing bli-1 is bypassed by enhancing the processing of dsRNA through the loss of ERI-1 or the overexpression of RDE-4.
source: Consistently, the requirement for NRDE-3 for silencing bli-1 is bypassed by enhancing the processing of dsRNA through the loss of ERI-1 or the overexpression of RDE-4.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The combined loss of both MUT-16 and RDE-10 eliminates all detectable silencing and this requirement cannot be overcome by enhancing dsRNA processing.
source: However, the combined loss of both MUT-16 and RDE-10 eliminates all detectable silencing and this requirement cannot be overcome by enhancing dsRNA processing.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1, 2, and 3.

claim: MUT-16 is detectable in the germline localized within perinuclear foci, but it is also found throughout the soma.
source: MUT-16 is detectable in the germline localized within perinuclear foci, but it is also found throughout the soma (Uebel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: MUT-16 is required for the silencing of all tested somatic targets except the muscle gene unc-22.
source: MUT-16 is required for the silencing of all tested somatic targets except the muscle gene unc-22, which showed residual silencing ('+++' vs '+' but not '-' in Zhang et al., 2011)
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: unc-22 is a particularly sensitive target for RNAi.
source: consistent with its early identification as a sensitive target for RNAi (Fire et al., 1998).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: RDE-10 has structural homology with the 3′–5′ exonuclease ERI-1.
source: Although the biochemical function of RDE-10 is unknown, it has structural homology with the 3′–5′ exonuclease ERI-1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: In eri-1(−); nrde-3(−) double mutants, a different 2° Argonaute is able to compensate for the lack of NRDE-3.
source: One explanation for these results is that in eri-1(−); nrde-3(−) double mutants (Figure 3G), a different 2° Argonaute is able to compensate for the lack of NRDE-3
evidence: This is a proposed explanation based on experimental data.

claim: In mut-16(−); eri-1(−) or rde-10(−); eri-1(−) double-mutants, the reduction of 2° siRNAs is too great to cause a detectable Bli-1 defect.
source: whereas in mut-16(−); eri-1(−) or rde-10(−); eri-1(−) double-mutants, the reduction of 2° siRNAs is too great to cause a detectable Bli-1 defect.
evidence: This is a proposed explanation based on experimental data.

claim: Multiple small RNA species of defined lengths and 5′-nt bias have been detected in C. elegans.
source: Multiple small RNA species of defined lengths and 5′-nt bias have been detected in C. elegans.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: 22G RNAs (2° siRNAs) are the most abundant small RNAs and arise from amplification downstream of exposure to dsRNA and in multiple endogenous small RNA pathways.
source: Of these, 22G RNAs (2° siRNAs) are the most abundant and arise from amplification downstream of exposure to dsRNA and in multiple endogenous small RNA pathways (Gu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Production of 2° siRNAs in response to dsRNA is eliminated in animals that lack both MUT-16 and RDE-10.
source: Our results suggest that production of 2° siRNAs in response to dsRNA is eliminated in animals that lack both MUT-16 and RDE-10 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: MUT-16 is thought to nucleate perinuclear foci in the germline that recruit many additional components.
source: While the precise mechanisms of amplification are unknown, MUT-16 is thought to nucleate perinuclear foci in the germline (Phillips et al., 2012; Uebel et al., 2018) that recruit many additional components – RDE-2, MUT-7, MUT-14, MUT-15, NYN-1, NYN-2, RDE-8, RDE-3/MUT-2, etc. (Phillips and Updike, 2022; Uebel et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: RDE-8 has a demonstrated role in the cleavage of mRNAs.
source: The roles of most of these proteins remain obscure, but RDE-8 (Tsai et al., 2015) and RDE-3/MUT-2 (Shukla et al., 2020) have demonstrated roles in the cleavage and pUGylation of mRNAs, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: RDE-3/MUT-2 has a demonstrated role in the pUGylation of mRNAs.
source: The roles of most of these proteins remain obscure, but RDE-8 (Tsai et al., 2015) and RDE-3/MUT-2 (Shukla et al., 2020) have demonstrated roles in the cleavage and pUGylation of mRNAs, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: RDE-10 and associated proteins play an independent role in the amplification of 2° siRNAs.
source: Yet, the observation of silencing in the absence of MUT-16 that is eliminated upon additional loss of RDE-10 suggests that RDE-10 and associated proteins (e.g., RDE-11 and RDE-12) play an independent role in the amplification of 2° siRNAs (Yang et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data and cited literature.

claim: The RdRP RRF-3 transcribes long antisense RNA from internal C nucleotides on template mRNA.
source: Current models for the production of 26G RNAs (Blumenfeld and Jose, 2016; Chaves et al., 2021) propose that the RdRP RRF-3 transcribes long antisense RNA from internal C nucleotides on template mRNA
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: The phosphatase PIR-1 converts the 5′ triphosphate of the RdRP product into 5′ mono phosphate.
source: the phosphatase PIR-1 converts the 5′ triphosphate of the RdRP product into 5′ mono phosphate
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: The template is trimmed by the 3′–5′ exonuclease ERI-1 to generate a blunt-ended dsRNA.
source: the template is then trimmed by the 3′–5′ exonuclease ERI-1 to generate a blunt-ended dsRNA
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: The blunt-ended dsRNA is cleaved by DCR-1 to generate the mature 26G RNAs that are bound by the Argonaute ERGO-1.
source: which is then cleaved by DCR-1 to generate the mature 26G RNAs that are bound by the Argonaute ERGO-1.
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: The detection of long pUG RNAs with no detectable shorter pUG RNAs upstream of sequences matching the dsRNA argues against the 3′ trimming of mRNA templates to generate shorter RNAs that then get pUGylated.
source: The detection of long pUG RNAs with no detectable shorter pUG RNAs upstream of sequences matching the dsRNA (Figure 6C) argues against the 3′ trimming of mRNA templates to generate shorter RNAs that then get pUGylated to become stabilized templates for RdRPs and against pUG RNA generation driven by successive rounds of 22G RNA production in somatic cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: RDE-10 has a conserved Maelstrom domain that shares homology with the DnaQ-H 3′–5′ exonuclease family.
source: RDE-10 has a conserved Maelstrom domain that shares homology with the DnaQ-H 3′–5′ exonuclease family (Zhang et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: The Maelstrom domain of RDE-10 shares high structural homology with the 3′–5′ exonuclease domain of ERI-1.
source: Intriguingly, the Maelstrom domain of RDE-10 shares high structural homology with the 3′–5′ exonuclease domain of ERI-1 (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C, left)
evidence: This is based on structural analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: ERI-1 can trim single-stranded RNA overhangs in vitro.
source: ERI-1 can trim single-stranded RNA overhangs in vitro (Kennedy et al., 2004)
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: ERI-1 is required for the production of 26G RNAs.
source: and is required for the production of 26G RNAs (Duchaine et al., 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: ERI-1 is required for the maturation of rRNAs.
source: and for the maturation of rRNAs (Gabel and Ruvkun, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: RDE-10 could interact with the Argonaute ERGO-1.
source: Furthermore, RDE-10 could interact with other parts of the RNA silencing machinery (e.g., the Argonaute ERGO-1 as seen using immunoprecipitation; Yang et al., 2012; Zhang et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: The 3′–5′ exonuclease SND1 trims the 3′ ends of miRNAs bound to AGO1 in Arabidopsis.
source: In support of such exonucleolytic trimming in conjunction with Argonaute binding, the 3′–5′ exonuclease SND1 has been shown to trim the 3′ ends of miRNAs bound to AGO1 in Arabidopsis (Chen et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: piRNA maturation in Drosophila and mice involves piwi-type Argonautes binding the 5′ end of the pre-piRNA followed by endonucleolytic cutting and exonucleolytic trimming.
source: Furthermore, piRNA maturation in Drosophila and mice suggests a model where piwi-type Argonautes bind the 5′ end of the pre-piRNA followed by endonucleolytic cutting and exonucleolytic trimming to generate consistently sized mature piRNAs (Stoyko et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Human ERI1 can trim Ago2-bound micro RNAs to 19-nt.
source: Finally, human ERI1 can trim Ago2-bound micro RNAs to 19-nt (Sim et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citation to published work.

claim: Production of 22G RNAs in response to dsRNA occurs through non-processive RdRPs making a heterogenous mixture of short RNAs, 2° Argonautes binding the 5′ end of these pre-secondary siRNA, and RDE-10 and/or associated protein(s) removing excess 3′ sequence to generate 22-nt siRNAs.
source: Therefore, we propose that the production of 22G RNAs in response to the addition of dsRNA occurs as follows: (1) non-processive RdRPs (e.g., RRF-1; Aoki et al., 2007) make a heterogenous mixture of short RNAs, (2) 2° Argonautes bind the 5′ end of these pre-secondary siRNA, and (3) RDE-10 and/or associated protein(s) remove excess 3′ sequence to generate 22-nt siRNAs that are effectively retained by the mature siRNA–Argonaute complex.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on inference from experimental data and cited literature.

claim: Plants have RdRPs that could be used to make 2° siRNAs.
source: Like C. elegans, plants (Sanan-Mishra et al., 2021) and some insects (Pinzón et al., 2019) have RdRPs that could be used to make 2° siRNAs
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Some insects have RdRPs that could be used to make 2° siRNAs.
source: Like C. elegans, plants (Sanan-Mishra et al., 2021) and some insects (Pinzón et al., 2019) have RdRPs that could be used to make 2° siRNAs
evidence: This is supported by citations to published work.

claim: Many animals, including humans, do not have RdRPs and thus are unlikely to produce 2° siRNAs.
source: but many other animals, including humans, do not have RdRPs and thus are unlikely to produce 2° siRNAs.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Silencing can fade despite the production of 2° siRNAs.
source: However, silencing can fade despite the production of 2° siRNAs (Figure 6A), highlighting the importance of dosage for all systems.
evidence: This is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: A drug that takes longer to cause an effect could have a more long-lasting effect.
source: In short, a drug that takes longer to cause an effect could have a more long-lasting effect.
evidence: This is an inference based on modeling results showing uncorrelated τkd and tkd.

claim: If two genes are at steady state, then the gene with higher mRNA turnover will be more difficult to knockdown because of higher rates of mRNA production.
source: If two genes are at steady state, then the gene with higher mRNA turnover will be more difficult to knockdown because of higher rates of mRNA production (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 4G.

claim: A gene undergoing upregulation of transcription, splicing, and/or mRNA export during the administration of the drug will be difficult to knockdown.
source: Similarly, in the absence of a steady state, a gene undergoing upregulation of transcription, splicing, and/or mRNA export during the administration of the drug will be difficult to knockdown (e.g., Figure 4F).
evidence: This is based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 4F.

claim: When a gene with a high threshold for silencing is targeted, it could rely on multiple regulators that act in parallel to contribute to silencing, making resistance through the mutation of any one regulator more likely.
source: When a gene with a high threshold for silencing is targeted, it could rely on multiple regulators that act in parallel to contribute to silencing (e.g., bli-1 in this study), making resistance through the mutation of any one regulator more likely and necessitating another round of drug development.
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data and modeling.

claim: Genes with a lower threshold may not require all the regulators for silencing, making them ideal targets that remain silenced despite single mutations in many regulators of RNAi.
source: In contrast, genes with a lower threshold may not require all the regulators for silencing (e.g., unc-22 in this study), making them ideal targets that remain silenced despite single mutations in many regulators of RNAi (e.g., RDE-10, MUT-16, or NRDE-3 in this study).
evidence: This is an inference based on experimental data.
